correctness.rationale: Eliseev proves B congruent to I modulo p throughout the standard orbit, so the normalized skew residue is integral modulo p. For a mutation the integral change-of-basis matrix reduces modulo p to the adjacent transposition because the mutation coefficient is divisible by p; conjugating B-B^T and dividing by p gives signed-permutation covariance. Sign changes act by diagonal congruence and Euler-form isometries leave the Gram matrix unchanged. Squaring the cyclic triangle product removes the orientation sign from relabeling. The Beilinson formula follows from Eliseev's Lemma 4, and exact enumeration gives the p=5 and p=7 distributions. The embedded verifier replays these calculations and exact mutation transformations.

value.rationale: The recent paper's central problem is to distinguish mutation orbits of numerical exceptional bases. The normalized-skew switching class retains substantially more of the newly discovered p^2 data than the yes/no test that all off-diagonal entries are nonzero. Its triangle-square fingerprint is inexpensive to compute, has an explicit closed form for the standard orbit, and can reject future candidate bases without requiring ranks or zero pairings. This is a natural structural lemma for the emerging orbit-separation problem rather than an arbitrary numerical slice.
